lessons.title: Find spaCR on GitHub, PyPI and conda-forge
lessons.description: Find the official package and installer sources, compare the release available on each channel, and choose the matching installation tutorial.
objectives: Find the official download pages.
Choose the installation route for your computer.
Open the matching installation tutorial.
lessons.prerequisite: Open a web browser and decide whether you want a desktop installer or a Python environment.

scenes.narration: Choose how you want to install spaCR. Use a desktop installer for a ready-to-launch application, pip for a Python virtual environment, or conda-forge for a Conda environment. Start from the official spaCR links shown here.

On PyPI, find spaCR and read the installation command beside the current release. Copy that command when you are ready to install into your Python environment. The pip tutorial shows how to create and activate that environment first.
Use Project links to open the documentation, source repository or issue tracker. Bookmark the documentation so you can return to the module walkthroughs while working in spaCR.
On GitHub, open the spaCR repository. Main contains the release source, and nightly contains the latest development work. For a packaged desktop installation, open Releases and choose a release.

Expand Assets and download the installer for Windows, macOS or Linux. Keep the checksum file from the same release if you want to verify the download. The Platform installers lesson walks through launching the installer and opening spaCR.
On conda-forge, open the spaCR package page and check the available version. Package channels can update at different times, so select the version available through the route you choose.
The conda-forge command installs spaCR into your active Conda environment. Follow the Conda lesson to create that environment, install the package and launch the application.
Continue with pip, Conda or Platform installers. Once spaCR opens, move to the Home lesson, then the pipeline overviews to choose a workflow for your data.

lessons.title: Installazione con Conda
lessons.description: Installa il pacchetto ufficiale conda-forge in un ambiente separato, verifica la versione effettiva del canale e riconosci le differenze dai tutorial attuali dei moduli.
objectives: Creare e attivare un ambiente Conda dedicato.
Verificare il pacchetto del canale, Qt e la diagnostica.
Scegliere pip o l’installer desktop più recente quando il canale mantiene l’interfaccia precedente.
lessons.prerequisite: Deve essere già installato un gestore compatibile con Conda. La registrazione verifica spaCR 1.5.0.4 da conda-forge su Linux, con Python 3.12.14 e Qt 6.11.2, il 10 settembre 2026. L’installazione pulita usa un nuovo percorso privato, solo conda-forge e la versione del canale fissata; le schede illustrano il procedimento equivalente con un ambiente con nome, senza simulare output d’installazione. La GUI reale conserva Home (63), non la struttura annidata di PyPI/installer 1.5.0.5. spacr-doctor supera la piccola prova di allocazione CUDA, ma segnala un avviso CZI facoltativo; non è un benchmark né una verifica di ogni analisi o formato. La cattura usa un profilo scuro privato con scala caratteri 1.5, il tour già chiuso e il precaricamento predefinito, senza l’opzione --no-setup non supportata. Altre piattaforme non sono state testate. La narrazione nei file di lavoro differisce da quella pubblicata: non si dichiara il riuso di audio identico.

lessons.title: Installare spaCR con pip
lessons.description: Crea un ambiente Python isolato, installa il pacchetto pubblico, verifica le dipendenze e avvia l’applicazione Qt installata.
objectives: Mantenere le dipendenze di spaCR in un ambiente Python dedicato.
Verificare il pacchetto installato, Qt e gli avvisi sulle funzioni facoltative.
Aprire Home e aggiornare consapevolmente l’ambiente corretto.
lessons.prerequisite: La lezione verifica spaCR 1.5.0.5 da PyPI su Linux con Python 3.12.13, non un’installazione modificabile del repository. Le schede dei comandi sono istruzioni, non output registrato; i comandi Windows e macOS non sono stati eseguiti qui. L’installazione pulita è terminata prima delle verifiche registrate. Le dipendenze di base attuali includono Qt. Doctor segnala un avviso CZI facoltativo; la prova di allocazione GPU è esplicitamente saltata. La cattura usa --no-setup, un profilo scuro privato con scala caratteri 1.5 e un tour già chiuso. Dimostra l’apertura e la chiusura normale di Home, non tutti i moduli, formati facoltativi, calcoli GPU o altre piattaforme.

lessons.title: Programmi di installazione per piattaforma
lessons.description: Scegli il programma ufficiale, comprendi la selezione automatica dell’acceleratore e le opzioni di riservatezza, quindi verifica l’ambiente Linux realmente installato.
objectives: Selezionare il programma ufficiale per il sistema operativo.
Distinguere l’accelerazione automatica dalla scelta esplicita della sola CPU.
Leggere le opzioni di riservatezza, le versioni installate e gli avvisi diagnostici.
lessons.prerequisite: Questa registrazione verifica il programma pubblico online per Linux x86-64 di spaCR 1.5.0.5, confrontato con la somma di controllo il 10 settembre 2026, con Python 3.12.13, Qt 6.11.2 e Torch 2.14.0+cu132. L’installazione reale è terminata prima delle immagini di verifica. Ha usato nuove cartelle private per ambiente ed eseguibile di avvio, librerie grafiche di sistema già presenti, --skip-system-deps e --no-launch; nessun ambiente o dipendenza di sistema preesistente è stato modificato. Le quattro schede sono istruzioni, non installazioni Windows/macOS registrate né output di terminale inventato. Le indicazioni Windows/macOS sono state controllate solo nel codice attuale dei programmi di installazione. La cattura usa un profilo scuro privato, scala del carattere 1.5, presentazione già chiusa, precaricamento su richiesta e --no-setup, che non esclude la domanda separata sulla riservatezza. Esc rifiuta quella finestra lasciando disattivate tutte le opzioni; le preferenze private sono state rilette per confermarlo. Doctor usa --no-gpu-probe; non si dichiara la verifica di allocazione, velocità, analisi o altre piattaforme. I tentativi di registrazione falliti sono conservati, non conteggiati come difetti dell’applicazione.

scenes.narration: Usa la versione ufficiale di spaCR su GitHub e scegli il programma per il tuo sistema operativo. I programmi online scaricano un ambiente Python privato e le dipendenze scientifiche; non serve un ambiente Conda esistente. In questo esempio Linux abbiamo confrontato il file scaricato con la somma di controllo della versione prima di eseguirlo.

I programmi online scaricano un ambiente Python privato e le dipendenze scientifiche; non serve un ambiente Conda esistente. In questo esempio Linux abbiamo confrontato il file scaricato con la somma di controllo della versione prima di eseguirlo.

lessons.title: Home screen and navigation
lessons.description: Open a module from Home, find its related tools and example data, then choose a pipeline to follow.
objectives: Choose a starting module for images, measurements or sequencing reads.
Find related tools and organism-specific assays.
Load an example, find help and open a pipeline overview.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open the desktop application.

scenes.narration: Home is your starting point. Click a tile to open a module, or use the sidebar on the left. Click Home in the sidebar to return here. The Core, Data, Tools and Assays tabs help you find the task you want to do.

For microscope images, begin with Mask to outline objects, then Measure to extract their features and crops. Annotate lets you label example objects, and Classify learns from those labels to score more objects. Map Barcodes reads sequencing data. Regression combines the resulting phenotype scores and guide counts to find associations.

Open Data to bring existing files into a project or work with results. Import accepts images, masks and measurement tables. Use Run Compare to compare runs, Experiment Design to prepare plate layouts, and QC to inspect recorded quality checks. Choose the tile that matches your next task.

Open Tools for image editing and exploration. Make Masks lets you edit masks and open the Cellpose Workbench. Align and Stitch combines overlapping image tiles. Image UMAP, Gate Editor and Graph Builder help you explore measurements and make plots. Open a module to find its related tools in the toolbar.

Open Assays and choose your organism: Toxoplasma, Plasmodium or Candida. Then choose an assay from that organism’s menu. For example, open Toxoplasma for plaque analysis or host–pathogen measurements. Follow the selected assay’s tutorial to prepare its images, masks and measurement inputs.

Open Classify and use Classifier family to choose your input. Select Computer Vision for object images, or Tabular Machine Learning for measured feature columns. The linked tutorials take you through training, evaluation and scoring for each family.

The toolbar in Classify opens Classifier Evaluation, Explain CV Model, Activation, Training Runs and Feature Explorer. Hover over an icon to see its name, then click it to open the tool. Use these views to inspect a model, compare training runs or explore important features.

To try a module, click Load test data when it is available. Wait for the download to finish, then review the filled inputs and settings. In Mask, click Live to inspect a field before pressing Run. Turn on Time for a time series or three-D for a volumetric image.

Type a module, setting or function name into the search field beside Help. Here, searching for Performance finds the matching Preferences page. Click a result to open its destination. API results open the documentation for the selected function.

In Preferences, choose a Performance profile for your computer. Laptop uses fewer resources; the higher profiles allow more caching and background work. Start with a modest profile if memory is limited. Your analysis settings stay under your control in each module.

Return to Home and click Pipeline overviews to choose a workflow. Start with spaCR screens for a pooled image-based screen, or choose an image-analysis or sequencing pathway for your data. The next tutorials show how those modules connect, and the module lessons then walk through each task.

lessons.title: Python API and batch commands
lessons.description: Find an analysis function, load saved settings, check the inputs and run spaCR from a terminal.
objectives: Find the installed batch commands and their Python functions.
Inspect a function signature and its API reference.
Check saved settings before running an analysis.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and activate its Python environment. Follow the Regression tutorial to prepare paired score/count tables and save the analysis settings. Use your own file paths in the commands.

scenes.narration: Activate the Python environment where you installed spaCR. Import spacr and print its version with the command shown. Keep the version with your analysis notes so you can reproduce the same run later.

Run spacr-run with dash dash list to find the available batch commands. The list shows each command key and its Python function. Choose the command for your task, such as mask, measure or regression. Use the desktop application for interactive tasks such as labelling images in Annotate.

Run spacr-run with dash dash describe followed by regression. Read the required inputs, defaults and function name. Here, the batch command calls perform_regression in spacr.ml. Open that function in the API reference to read its parameters and returned results.

In Python, import the function you need and inspect its signature. This example imports build_report from spacr.report. Look up the same name in the API reference, prepare the required arguments, and call the function from your script or notebook.

Save the settings from your module workflow, then pass the file with dash dash settings. Add dash dash dry-run to check the configuration and input paths. In this Regression example, the settings pair phenotype scores with guide counts for each plate. Read the messages and correct any missing inputs before continuing.

To execute the analysis, run the same command without dash dash dry-run. Follow the console until the command finishes, then inspect the outputs described by that module’s tutorial and API page. Keep the settings file, input tables, package version and console log with the results.

lessons.title: Mask: segment images and inspect the results
lessons.description: Load microscope images, choose segmentation settings, preview objects and save masks for measurement.
objectives: Load the microscopy example and identify its intensity channels.
Compare model settings and object-size filters in Live preview.
Run segmentation, inspect overlays and find the merged outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Mask and choose Load test data. For your own images, prepare a source folder with consistent filenames and known channel identities. This example uses nucleus channel 0, cell channel 1 and pathogen channel 2, with an additional intensity channel 3.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Mask. Use this module to outline cells, nuclei and pathogens in microscope images. This walkthrough processes two-dimensional images. The Time, three-dimensional and OPS workflows have their own tutorials.

Click Load test data and wait for the microscopy example to load. Check Source before continuing. For your own images, select their folder and confirm that the filenames identify the plate, well, field and channel.

Check the channel assignments against the images. In this example, nucleus intensity is channel zero, cell intensity is channel one, and pathogen intensity is channel two. Channel three is an additional intensity image. Choose only the object types present in your experiment.
Turn on Live and select a field. Inspect the image and proposed masks together before running the full folder. Try several fields that represent the range of image quality in your experiment.

Open Live settings and choose the model for the object you want to segment. Set the approximate object diameter and run the preview. Compare the outlines with the image, paying attention to missed objects and objects joined together.

Use the minimum-area filter to hide objects smaller than the chosen number of pixels. Increasing it removes small labels from the preview. This filter updates an existing mask result, so you can compare size cutoffs quickly.

Change diameter when the model is splitting or joining objects at the wrong scale, then run the preview again. Check the boundaries as well as the object count. Restore the settings you want to use before moving to the batch run.

For a small first run, select two test images, keep Plot on, and review the cell, nucleus and pathogen flow thresholds. Here they are zero point four. Check the output and original-image retention settings, then click Run.

Follow the console and inspect any failed fields or missing plots. The merged folder contains the image intensities and final object labels. Keep its plane-layout metadata with the arrays so Measure can identify each channel and mask.

If an overlay export is missing, the linked plotting helper can export the saved arrays separately. Extract the helper and choose this run’s merged folder. Keep the layout file in place; the helper uses it to check the intensity and mask planes.
Run the helper with the merged folder as its source and a new output folder as its destination. It saves a separate overlay for each image array. Open the saved PNG files to inspect the results.

Review the outlines on each intensity channel and the combined mask view. Check small objects, touching cells and missed regions. Keep the input images, settings, masks and quality reports together, then continue to Measure to extract object features and crops.

lessons.title: Measure: extract object features and crops
lessons.description: Load images with masks, inspect objects, choose crop settings and save measurements for annotation and classification.
objectives: Identify intensity channels and mask planes in the example.
Inspect fields and choose saved-crop normalization deliberately.
Run Measure and locate the database, object crops and figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Use the merged outputs from Mask, or choose Load test data in Measure. The example supplies sixteen fields with intensity planes 0–3 and cell, nucleus and pathogen masks in planes 4, 5 and 6.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Measure. Start with images that already have object masks. Measure extracts features such as area and intensity, pairs related objects, and can save individual object crops for Annotate and Classify.

Click Load test data and wait for the example to load, or select your own merged project. Check the plane mapping: this example has four intensity channels followed by cell, nucleus and pathogen masks in planes four, five and six.

To inspect these sixteen-bit example crops, turn Normalize on before opening Live. This makes the preview easier to see. Remember that this main setting also affects saved crops; we will switch it off before this batch run.
Turn on Live and choose a field. Inspect the object crops and their mask relationships. Scroll through the categories and enlarge the preview if needed to see the boundaries clearly.

Use the displayed-channel selector to inspect one intensity channel at a time. Channel zero shows a grayscale view; All channels restores the combined view. This selector changes the preview without changing the labels or batch channel mapping.

Choose another field and compare its objects. Review the segmentation-quality banner before measuring the project. If masks are missing or joined incorrectly, correct them or adjust Mask before continuing.

Turn Live off and restore Normalize off for this example. Choose normalization deliberately when saving crops: per-crop scaling changes the intensity differences visible to a later image classifier. Keep the original merged arrays for quantitative measurements.

Enable saving measurements and object crops, keep Plot on, and choose the crop size and output channels. Use one worker for this example. Leave Test mode off to process all sixteen supplied fields, then click Run.
Follow the console until the run completes. Check which fields succeeded and inspect any failures before proceeding. Keep the settings saved with this run so you can reproduce the measurements.

Use the figure list to compare objects before and after filtering. Size filters and parent-child relationships can change which objects are measured. Drag the divider to give the figures more space and inspect any unexpected changes.

Inspect the crop figure, then locate measurements.db in the measurements folder and the saved object images in the project’s crop output. Keep the database and image paths together. Continue to Annotate to label example objects, or to Classify when you already have labelled training data.

lessons.title: Annotate: label objects and save your annotations
lessons.description: Load example crops, choose an annotation column, label objects, adjust the view and prepare your labels for classification.
objectives: Load saved crops or stream crops from merged images.
Choose an annotation column, assign and clear labels, and save your changes.
Adjust channel colours and review class counts and coverage.
Find Agreement and the image and feature training routes.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Annotate from Home. Use Load test data and choose Load for the example crops and measurements database. For your own project, use the folder containing its measurements database and crops or merged images.

scenes.narration: Open Annotate from Home. The grid shows individual objects from your project. You will label these objects and save the labels in the measurements database.
Click Load test data and choose Load. This downloads the example image crops and their measurements database, then opens them in Annotate.
Choose Stream when you want to read crops directly from merged images. Choose Load for already exported crops. We will use Load for this walkthrough.
To open your own data, click Open source and select the plate folder containing measurements and the image data. The grid then loads the objects from that project.
Inspect the crop grid. Use the page controls to browse the objects. Adjust the crop size if you need a closer view or want more objects on each page.
Open Settings and choose an annotation column. Create a new column to keep this labelling task separate from existing annotations. Decide what each class represents before you start.
Left-click a crop to assign class one. Right-click assigns class two. Click the same class again to clear it. The coloured ring shows the label, and the white ring marks the focused crop.
Press Next to move to the next page and submit your labels for saving. Wait for saving to finish before closing the application.

Press Back to return to the previous page and check your labels. You can also use keys one to nine to assign classes and zero to clear a label. The on-screen legend lists the navigation and undo shortcuts.
Open Class counts to see how many objects you have labelled in each class. Use this to find classes that need more examples.
Open Coverage to see how your annotations are distributed across the project. Include examples from the conditions and image groups you want the classifier to recognize.
To clear a label, click the same class again. Move to the next page to save the change, then return to check the cleared crop.
In Settings, Channel colours selects the display palette. Display order assigns source channels to the colour slots. Choose a view that makes your classes easy to distinguish.
Here is the CMY palette. You can return to RGB through the same settings. Keep the view consistent while comparing and labelling objects.
Open Annotator Agreement from the icon at the top right to compare annotation columns. Use it to find objects where reviewers assigned different labels.
When your labels are ready, open Train. Choose images for an image classifier or measured features for a tabular classifier. The linked Classify lessons explain the training settings.
Suggest can propose labels for you to review. Retrain updates the model after you add labels, and Rounds helps you follow that review cycle. Check suggested labels before accepting them.
Generate annotation database creates a crop set from suitable source data. Use it when preparing a new annotation project; the downloaded example already includes the crops and database needed here.
Open Console to check source-loading and save messages. Your annotation column is stored in the project database and can be selected when you prepare training data in Classify.
For help with a setting, open spaCR AI in Console after configuring a provider in Preferences. When you have finished labelling, continue to Classify with your project and chosen annotation column.

lessons.title: Classify: train an image classifier
lessons.description: Prepare labelled image crops, choose the computer-vision family, train a small model and find its predictions.
objectives: Prepare the downloadable image-classification example.
Choose the model, image channels and training settings.
Keep wells separate and inspect saved models and predictions.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measured example through Annotate using Load test data, then Load. Keep its plate1 folder with measurements/measurements.db and the png crops. Download Classify_existing_split_example.zip below and extract the helper. In your spaCR environment, run prepare_classify_split.py --source /path/to/plate1 --destination /path/to/new_split. Select the new_split folder in Classify. The helper is for this four-well example; it copies 64 labelled RGB crops into train and test folders.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify and choose Computer Vision, Torch. This family learns from labelled object crops and saves a model that can score other crops. Follow the Annotate lesson first to download the example images and their labels.

In Annotate, choose Load test data, then Load. Keep the plate folder containing measurements and PNG crops. For your own data, start with crops from Measure and assign the classes you want to learn in Annotate.

Download the linked example ZIP and extract prepare_classify_split.py. Run it in your spaCR environment with source pointing to the example plate folder and destination pointing to a new folder. The helper prepares sixty-four labelled images for this exercise.

Open the new folder and its manifest. The train and test directories each contain two class folders. The manifest lists each copied image and its well. Keep whole wells on one side of the split when images from the same well share experimental conditions.

Return to Classify and choose the prepared folder as Source. Select the parent containing train and test. Keep that prepared folder for the rest of this lesson so the model and its output files stay together.

Turn Generate training dataset off because the helper has already prepared the split. Enable Train and Test. Leave application to the full dataset off for this first run. The model uses class indices zero and one for the two class folders.

Choose ResNet18, image size one hundred twenty-eight, all three RGB channels, batch size eight and one epoch. Set loader workers to two, with pretrained weights and augmentation off for this short example. Epochs controls how many times training passes through its input images.

Set validation fraction to one half, keep grouping by well and leave the leakage checks enabled. Validation monitors the model during training; the separate test folder is used for the final assessment. Check the reported well assignments before interpreting the scores.

Turn Plot on, clear the settings search and press Run. Watch the console for dataset loading, the resolved split, training progress and output paths. Wait for training and testing to finish before opening the saved results.

Open Figures to inspect loss and accuracy. One epoch gives a quick first pass. Compare the test results across classes before increasing training time. If predictions favour only one class, review the labels, class balance and input channels before using the model on a larger dataset.

Open model, resnet18, rgb, epochs underscore one inside the prepared folder. Keep the checkpoint, model card and result tables together. Use the saved predictions to review errors, then continue to Classifier Evaluation or Activation Maps to inspect the model further.

lessons.title: Classify: learn from measured features
lessons.description: Load measurements, define classes, train a tabular classifier and inspect object scores and plate summaries.
objectives: Select the tabular family and a measured project.
Define classes and choose feature channels, model size and held-out wells.
Find model outputs, object predictions and summary figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Use Load test data in Classify and choose Load, then confirm the downloaded plate folder with Choose source data. For your own project, run Measure first. The example uses columnID values c1 and c2 as two classes; use labels appropriate to your experiment when working with your own data.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify and choose Tabular Machine Learning. This family uses the object measurements saved by Measure. It produces a fitted model and a score for each object with the required measurements.
Click Load test data and choose Load. Wait for the measured example to download. For your own data, select the project folder created by Measure, including its measurements database.

Use Choose source data to confirm the downloaded plate folder. Select the folder containing measurements. This gives the classifier access to the object tables and the metadata used to define classes.

Choose metadata as the class basis and define two Classes using column I D values c1 and c2. These labels distinguish the two plate columns in the example. To train from your own cell annotations, choose the annotation basis and the label column you created in Annotate.

Set Channel of interest to one for the example. This controls which channel-specific measurement features enter the model. For your own experiment, select the channel that contains the signal relevant to your classes.

Choose Random Forest, sixteen estimators and two worker jobs. Estimators controls the number of trees. More trees increase fitting work. Leave feature pruning and cross-validation off for this first pass; you can compare those choices after you have a working baseline.

Set Test size to one tenth and keep grouping by well. spaCR holds out complete wells, so the final fraction of objects can differ from the requested fraction. Read the resolved split in the console and make sure it suits your experiment.

Enable Plot, clear the search and press Run. The console shows feature filtering, the training and test split, model fitting and the saved output paths. Wait for the run to finish before comparing its scores.

Find the results under results, random_forest, channel underscore one. The database stores the predicted class in predictions and the class-one probability in ml_pred. Objects missing required measurements can remain unscored; inspect missing values when exporting a summary.

Browse the feature-importance figures and plate heatmap. With Predictions and mean grouping, a well value is the average of its binary predicted classes. Use the saved object scores for detailed review, and compare held-out performance before applying the classifier to another experiment.

lessons.title: Map Barcodes: from sequencing reads to counts
lessons.description: Load paired reads and library references, find barcode positions, apply the settings and save guide counts.
objectives: Download a small paired-read example and select matching reference tables.
Inspect barcode positions and orientation before applying a proposal.
Run mapping and inspect count and quality-control outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose Load test data in Map Barcodes. The example uses SRR33531217 reads, the matching primers_3 column and row tables, and guide references. Use reference tables matching your own library when processing other reads.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Map Barcodes. The inputs are sequencing reads and reference tables that name the barcodes in your library. The output counts each observed combination, ready for sequencing quality control and downstream analysis.
Click Load test data and select both mates of the first archive run. Limit each file to ten thousand reads for this example, then wait for the paired sample to download.

Select the matching column, row and guide reference tables. Each table pairs barcode names with sequences. Keep those names consistent with the plate layout and guide identifiers used by the rest of your analysis.
Open Find barcodes and start the search. The preview samples both mates and checks barcode positions and orientations. Wait for the results before changing the main form.

Compare Observed with By chance, then inspect the proposed orientation, offset and verdict for each barcode. Prefer positions supported by many reads and distinct expected references. Open the verdict explanation if the result is uncertain.

Inspect the guide results for both mates. In this example, read one supports the reverse-complemented guide sequence and read two supports the stored orientation. Use the results for your library and read pair when choosing an orientation.

Check the row barcode as well. Here, read one supports its reverse complement and read two supports the stored sequence. Review column, guide and row together so the complete combination identifies the intended well and guide.

Open the read viewer to inspect individual reads. Use the colour legend to find the column, guide, row and anchor segments. Check that the proposed positions agree with the expected library structure.

Review the proposed extraction settings, then click Apply these settings to copy them into the form. The example uses an extraction window of eighty-nine bases. Check the updated fields before starting the run.

Follow the orientation notes when selecting your final reference files. For this example, select reverse-complemented copies of the row and guide references and keep the column reference as stored. Preserve every barcode name when preparing those copies.

Choose the downloaded read pair, two workers and chunks of one thousand reads. Enable annotated-read saving if you want to inspect individual assignments. Click Run; this mapping workflow uses the CPU.

When mapping finishes, inspect unique_combinations.csv and the quality-control outputs. The count table links column, row and guide names with read counts. Review unmatched and ambiguous assignments in Barcode QC, then pair these counts with phenotype scores in Regression.

lessons.title: Regression: from paired tables to results
lessons.description: Pair phenotype scores with guide counts, choose an inference method, run the example and explore guide and gene results.
objectives: Load paired score/count tables and choose an output folder.
Set the inference method, reporting level and analysis unit.
Run the example and inspect results with the accompanying diagnostics.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Regression and choose Load test data to obtain four paired score/count tables. Use a new output folder. A measurement database is optional for this score-and-count analysis; object-level views require the corresponding measured data and images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression. This module relates phenotype scores to guide abundance. Start with a score table and a count table for each plate, then choose how to test and report associations.
In Input Tables, click Load test data and wait for the example to load. It provides four score tables and four count tables, paired by plate.
Inspect each paired row and check the plate name, score file and count file. Leave the optional measurement-database column empty for this example. Choose a new output folder for the analysis.

Switch to All settings and use the search box to find Inference. Choose nonparametric for this guide-permutation example. Use a parametric method when your question and design call for fitting predictors together.
Level chooses which results to report. Select both to obtain guide-level and gene-level results. Keep these testing families separate when reviewing adjusted significance.

Choose well as the analysis unit for this example. Review the response column, transformations, controls and excluded wells. Adapt these settings to the design of your own screen before running new data.
Minimum guide support controls how many wells must contain a guide before it is tested. Set it to two to follow this small example. Choose an appropriate support requirement for your experiment.

Set one hundred and ninety-nine permutations for a quick first run. More permutations give finer empirical p-value resolution and take longer. Choose a larger count when your final analysis requires it.

Set the permutation seed to zero to repeat the same randomization. Keep the example’s plate blocks and row and column nuisance terms. For your own data, choose blocks that respect which observations can be exchanged under the experimental design.
Choose none for Annotation source to run the example without gene-annotation lookup. For another screen, select annotations that match its organism and identifier system.

Clear the search, check the paired inputs and output folder, then click Run. Follow the console as the module aligns the tables, filters guides and calculates the results. Diagnostic figures are generated with the analysis.

When the run finishes, open Runs and select the saved analysis. Confirm the folder and settings before comparing it with another run. Rerun the analysis after changing settings if you want new results.

Open Results and use Level to switch between guide and gene results. Inspect the result table and interactive views. The saved results_grna.csv and results_gene.csv files contain the corresponding tables for further analysis.

Open the p-values view and the Diagnostics tool. Review the result distribution together with the permutation resolution, testing family and design warnings. Resolve important diagnostic concerns before interpreting associations.

Use the toolbar to open Volcano Explorer, Hit List or Investigate Hit for the next step. Their tutorials show how to inspect selected results. Keep the input tables, saved settings, result files and diagnostic reports together when sharing the analysis.

lessons.title: Make Masks: edit labels and prepare training images
lessons.description: Open image-mask pairs, inspect and edit objects, save measurements and create paired training crops.
objectives: Open images with matching instance masks and inspect objects in the magnifier.
Measure paired fields and save an object-feature database.
Correct labels with Undo, drawing, division and size filters.
Save curated masks and create image-mask crops for training.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare a folder of two-dimensional images with matching instance-label TIFFs in a masks subfolder. Each mask uses the image filename stem. Work on a copy when practising edits and recropping. The example uses ER images and cell masks from Measure’s downloadable microscopy project.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Make Masks in Tools. Choose this editor to inspect and correct individual image masks. Open the folder of paired images and labels before choosing an editing tool.
Select the image folder. For this example, use the ER intensity images and corresponding cell masks from the Measure sample. Keep the image and mask dimensions equal and their filenames paired.

The editor loads the image and its matching mask from the masks subfolder. Coloured labels identify individual objects. Check that the outlines follow the image boundaries. If a companion mask is missing, start with an empty mask and draw the objects you need.
Open Magnifier settings. Select Otsu and Region under the mouse to preview threshold-based objects around the pointer. Choose a model-based mode when thresholding does not separate your objects well.

Turn on Magnifier and hover over an object to enlarge its preview. Move across several objects to inspect the proposed outlines. Click to add the outlined objects when they look correct, or switch Magnifier off to continue editing.

Click Features to measure image-mask pairs. Add a row for each field and choose the intensity images and corresponding object masks. Check manual assignments if automatic filename matching leaves files unassigned.
For each row, select the ER intensity image in Channel 1 and its matching label image in Cell mask. Repeat for the second field. Use the original intensity images to measure fluorescence.

Review both rows, then choose the measurement settings. This example uses one worker, a minimum cell size of one pixel and no saved PNG crops. Increase the size cutoff to exclude small objects when appropriate for your experiment. Click Measure.

When measurement finishes, open the output folder. The measurements folder contains measurements.db with the object features for both fields. Keep the database with its source images, masks and settings, then close Features to return to editing.

Choose the tool that matches the correction. Brush adds pixels, Erase removes pixels and Erase object removes a whole label. Draw adds an outlined object; Divide splits one. Zoom helps you inspect boundaries before making changes.

Choose Erase object and click inside the object you want to remove. Check the updated outline and object count. Use this for an unwanted label, such as debris or an object outside your analysis criteria.
Click Undo to restore the deletion. Redo applies it again. Use these history controls to compare an edit with the previous mask, then return to the version you want to keep.

Select Draw and trace a closed boundary around a missing object. The editor fills it with a new label. In this practice step the outline is in the background, so undo it before saving. For training data, trace the actual object boundary.

Use Divide when two touching objects share one label. Draw a cut across the whole joined region and inspect the separated labels. Undo the split if it cuts through one object or leaves an incorrect boundary.

Adjust Display percentiles to make dim structures easier to inspect. These controls change the image view while preserving raw intensity values and labels. Return to a consistent display when comparing fields.

Set the minimum and maximum object areas, then press Filter to remove labels outside those bounds. Choose bounds that fit your objects and inspect what was removed. The filter edits the mask, so use Undo if the cutoff removes useful objects.

After reviewing the edits, click Save mask. Reset size bounds to zero to disable them before moving to another field if needed. Preserve the source images and keep the saved curation record with the edited masks.

Use the header tools for the next step. Train Cellpose learns from your curated image-mask pairs; Mask the whole folder applies a model to a folder of images. Follow the linked tutorial for the workflow you need.

The header also opens Model Compare, Model Zoo, Curate and Open in napari. Use Model Compare to inspect masks side by side, Model Zoo to choose weights, and the curation tools to review or edit more examples.

Choose Recrop and drag a box around the objects you want in a smaller training field. This writes a new image and matching mask. Objects cut by the boundary are dropped, so leave space around complete objects and inspect the crop.
Click Next to open the new crop. The parent image and mask are retained in recropped_originals for recovery. Review the crop and its labels before adding it to your training dataset.

To detect objects in the current field, select the Cellpose model and review its settings. This example uses cpsam, normalization on, cell-probability threshold zero and flow threshold zero point four. Check whether detections will replace existing labels or be added to them.

Click Object detection and compare the resulting outlines with the image. Here the model selects the partial object at the upper left instead of the central cell. Undo that replacement and adjust the model settings before trying again.

Open Cell probability to inspect the foreground score map. Use it to see which regions the model supports. Change the foreground threshold when useful, then run detection again to produce a new result.

Open Flows to inspect the directional view. The flow-consistency threshold controls which detected objects are retained: lower values are stricter, and zero disables this check. Compare the final masks after each setting change.

Undo restores the labels from before the detection. Keep the mask that best follows the image, then save it. Continue through the remaining fields and inspect each result before including it in training.
Keep curated images and same-stem masks together. Use Train Cellpose to learn from those pairs, or return to Features or Measure to extract measurements. The related tutorials show each next step.

lessons.title: Image UMAP: explore measurements with image crops
lessons.description: Select measurement tables, build a UMAP embedding and click points to inspect the corresponding objects.
objectives: Load a measured project and choose its feature tables.
Control neighbourhood size, point spacing and the sampled row count.
Run the embedding, inspect crops and find saved results.
lessons.prerequisite: Follow Annotate and choose Load test data, then Load, to obtain the measured example and its image crops. Keep the downloaded plate folder. For your own data, complete Measure with saved crops before opening Image UMAP.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Image UMAP. Use it to explore similarities between measured objects while viewing their image crops. Start with a project containing a measurements database and the crops saved by Measure.

Under Source, choose Add project folders and select the example plate folder downloaded through Annotate. Review the available databases, rows and shared columns. You can add more project folders when you want to compare several datasets.

Choose the tables whose features you want to compare. For this example, select cell, cytoplasm, nucleus and pathogen measurements. Leave Resnet features off to use the existing measurements. Review missing-data and correlated-feature settings before running.
Set Row limit to four hundred for a quick first view and use two workers. Row limit controls how many objects enter the embedding. Increase it when you are ready to explore more of the dataset.

Choose UMAP as the reduction method. Each point will represent an object using two plotted coordinates. You can explore PCA through its linked tool when you want a linear projection and feature loadings.

Set Neighbours to fifteen and Minimum distance to zero point one. Neighbours controls the size of the neighbourhood used to build the map. Minimum distance controls how closely points can pack in the displayed embedding.
Set Random seed to forty-two so repeated runs with the same inputs and settings are easier to compare. Save your chosen feature tables and preprocessing settings alongside the seed.
Clustering assigns labels to groups after the embedding is built. This example uses DBSCAN with noise removal off. Inspect the crops within any group before using its label in a later analysis.
Enable Plot images and Plot points. Use twelve small crop images so the overview remains readable. You can inspect individual objects more closely in the interactive view after fitting.
Press Run and watch the console for feature preparation and embedding progress. Wait for the completed result. If you change the input tables or reduction settings, run again to produce a new map.

Inspect the embedding in Figures and open the results folder reported in the console. Keep the saved figure, selected measurement rows, metadata and cluster labels together so you can trace an interesting group back to its objects.
Enable Interactive to explore the fitted map. Zoom into a region and click its points. The view uses the completed embedding, so you can inspect different objects without fitting it again.

Click a point to show its crop in the side panel. Use the displayed object path to connect the image to its source record. Compare morphology across nearby points and across distant regions of the map.

Click another point to compare its crop. The sidebar also provides selection labelling and cluster-label propagation. Those controls save annotations, so choose the intended label and selection before applying them.

Open Image Scatter from the Image UMAP header to compare selected features directly, or open PCA for a linear projection. Continue with the linked tutorials for their input settings and saved outputs.

lessons.title: Activation Maps: inspect an image classifier’s saliency maps
lessons.description: Select a trained classifier and matching image crops, compare channel and image saliency, and open the saved maps.
objectives: Match the crop archive, model and preprocessing settings.
Run channel saliency with an image overlay.
Compare image saliency and locate the saved grids.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a trained image-classification checkpoint and a TAR archive of compatible image crops. Retain the crop-format marker when present and follow the model card’s channel order, image size and normalization. The example uses four RGB crops from Annotate and a ResNet18 model from Classify. Train or obtain a model whose preprocessing is known before starting.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then Activation Maps. This tool shows where a trained image classifier’s prediction is sensitive to the input pixels. Start with the model and an archive of crops prepared in the same way as its training data.

Select the crop archive in Dataset. This example contains four RGB cell crops from Annotate. Include the crop-format marker when packaging the images, and keep their filenames so you can connect each map to its original object.
Select the trained model and choose its model type. Here the model is ResNet eighteen. Read its model card and set Image size to one hundred and twenty-eight to match the training input.
Set Channels to the order expected by the model. In this example the selector uses one, two and three for the RGB input. Preserve that order when comparing maps from different images.
Set Normalize input to match training. The separate display normalization controls how the image appears in the saved overlay. Keep both settings consistent when comparing runs.
Choose saliency channel and enable Overlay, Plot and Save. This produces separate channel maps over the images. For the four-crop example, use a batch size of four and one worker, then click Run.
Follow the console until processing finishes. If the Figures panel is empty, open the output folder and inspect the saved batch grids. Check error messages and the saved results before continuing.

Open batch_0_grid.png from the method’s batch_grids folder. Match each occupied slot with its source crop; unused slots may be blank. The corner labels are model predictions. Compare salient regions with the original image and known object boundaries.
To compare a combined map, select saliency image and turn Overlay off. Run the same images again with the same preprocessing. Keep the two methods’ outputs in their respective folders.

Open the second saved grid. Image saliency combines the channel sensitivities into one map for each crop. Compare the highlighted regions with the channel maps. The displayed colours indicate the map scale; interpreting them requires checking the model and image context.

Leave Correlation off for this first walkthrough. Review examples from different classes, including prediction errors, before interpreting patterns. Use Classifier Evaluation to assess performance on independently held-out data.

Keep the input archive, model and model card, settings, maps and output database together. Return to the original crops to investigate unexpected regions, or compare another method using the same inputs.

lessons.title: Tracciamento temporale
lessons.description: Esegui otto fotogrammi sintetici dal flusso annidato in Mask e confronta i collegamenti delle maschere in Track preview.
objectives: Trovare Timelapse in Mask e conservare asse temporale e immagini originali.
Confrontare tracce iniziali, frammentate e ripristinate sulle stesse maschere.
Distinguere indicatori, riproduzione, inferenza e movimento biologico misurato.
lessons.prerequisite: Scegli Help > Demos > Timelapse demo in una nuova cartella: otto tempi sintetici di 256 per 256 pixel, nucleo nel canale 0 e cellula nel canale 1. Attiva Plot e Keep original images; i sedici TIFF restano invariati. Lo ZIP contiene piani cellulari esatti di questa esecuzione, non dati acquisiti né verità di riferimento. Seleziona separatamente image_sequences/field_A01 e label_sequences/field_A01, canale 0, otto fotogrammi e un campo. La soglia 0.1 dà sedici tracce complete; 1.0 ne dà 128 da un fotogramma. Ripristina 0.1, attendi e premi Re-link: la digitazione può avviare un valore intermedio. Non premere Propagate settings, che non trasferisce la soglia IoU. Sono dichiarati gli avvisi su flow threshold, tabella delle relazioni e stato delle impostazioni. Nessuna validazione biologica o velocità fisica. lessons.title: Motility assay
lessons.description: Measure movement from tracked objects, inspect track filters, and save per-frame and per-well results.
objectives: Load a project containing tracked merged arrays.
Choose mask planes, track filters and acquisition units.
Run the analysis and find the movement tables and plots.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete a Timelapse run, or download and extract SYNTHETIC_motility_tracks.zip. Select the folder containing merged. The example has eight frames, nucleus intensity in channel 0, cell intensity in channel 1, tracked cell masks in plane 2 and nucleus masks in plane 3. It has no pathogen mask or physical calibration.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Measure, then use Time to open Motility Assay. Start with tracked images from Timelapse, or download the example archive below to follow along.
Extract the example and set Source to the folder containing merged. Choose cells as the tracked objects, nucleus channel zero and cell channel one. Leave the pathogen channel unset for this example.

Turn on Live to open Motility preview and choose the same project folder. Use the preview to inspect tracks and try filters before running the full analysis. Keep Propagate settings off while exploring temporary choices.

Set two intensity channels, tracked mask plane two, and pathogen mask plane minus one, meaning none. Preview all eight frames. In the preview, set both calibration values to zero for this uncalibrated example, then click Run preview.

At minimum track length three, the example has sixteen usable tracks. Review the trajectories, length distribution and speed summary. Speed is about one point four pixels per frame because the example has no acquisition scale or interval.
Min track length sets how many frames an object must span to enter the summary. Increase it to exclude brief tracks, and watch the retained count. Keep it at three for this eight-frame example.

Drop over-straight tracks excludes tracks above the chosen straightness threshold. Straightness is net displacement divided by total path length. Compare the retained tracks and plots before choosing a threshold; leave this filter off when straight movement is part of your experiment.

For acquired data, enter pixels per micrometre and seconds per frame from your microscope and acquisition metadata. With both values, the preview can express speed in micrometres per minute. To try the conversion on this teaching example, two pixels per micrometre and sixty seconds per frame change the mean to about zero point seven. Those are example values, not measured calibration.

Set the full analysis form’s pixel scale and frame interval as well; preview edits are separate until you propagate them. Check the chosen object, channels and filters before starting the run. Keep the acquisition values with your results.

Leave Reuse existing measurements off for the first run and enable the quality-control graphs. With no pathogen channel, leave infection quality control disabled. Click Run and follow progress in the console.

When the run finishes, open measurements, then measurements.db in the project folder. The selected table contains per-frame observations; its well_motility companion summarizes movement by well. Inspect the saved plots and their units before comparing conditions or exporting figures.

lessons.title: Train Cellpose: coppie verificate e procedura esplicita tramite API
lessons.description: Trova Train nel Cellpose Workbench, riconosci il difetto di importazione della sorgente e segui un vero addestramento Python di due epoche su sei coppie scaricabili immagine/maschera cellulare.
objectives: Trovare Train e Apply dentro Make Masks, non come tessere Home separate.
Verificare nomi abbinati e distinguere etichette esistenti da riferimenti revisionati.
Riconoscere l’importazione parziale e separare API e GUI difettosa.
Esaminare input, riscaldamento, pesi modificati e percorso verificato.
Distinguere perdita, valori di test segnaposto e lettura dei pesi dall’accuratezza indipendente.
lessons.prerequisite: Usa sei coppie, script registrato e manifesto collegati. I ritagli conservano intensità cellulare canale 1 e maschera cellulare piano 4 da campi reali; piano 6 significa patogeno. Etichette e oggetti tagliati NON sono riferimenti revisionati indipendentemente. Train perde ancora src e mantiene model_name=new_model pur importando i numeri; nessun training GUI parte. La chiamata spacr.submodules.train_cellpose usa destinazione nuova, due epoche, minibatch 1, learning_rate=1e-5, weight_decay=1e-5, target_size=512, senza aumento extra spaCR. normalize=False disattiva i percentili spaCR, non la divisione per il massimo né la normalizzazione Cellpose. Cellpose ruota/ridimensiona e usa patch interne di 256. Seed 19 iniziale, casualità interna conservata. CUDA al 65% su RTX 3090 e guardia RAM 100 GiB adatta soltanto a questa macchina. Verificati 3,145,728 valori e dodici pannelli; tutte le sei coppie restano nel training. Tassi 0 e 1.1111111111111112e-6; 345 di 347 tensori addestrabili modificati. Perdita salita da 1.496740683913231 a 1.5215517828861873. Nessun test, quindi gli zeri sono segnaposto. Checkpoint sotto models/cellpose_model/models letto con weights_only=True; il riepilogo omette il secondo models. Leggere non significa inferenza o accuratezza. Figura reale in visualizzatore esterno, mai inserita nella GUI. Originali, tentativi falliti e blocco GUI conservati. Nessuna richiesta AI, risposta, approvazione scientifica o pubblicazione.
